title: India's First Dengue Vaccine Could Reach Private Hospitals in Early 2027
excerpt: Dr Reddy's will distribute Takeda's Qdenga in India's private market from early 2027 — the first dengue vaccine approved in a country that carries a third of the global burden.
body:
• Dr Reddy's Laboratories has signed an exclusive agreement with Japan's Takeda to distribute Qdenga — India's first approved dengue vaccine — in the country's private market from the first half of 2027.
  • Qdenga (TAK-003) is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine protecting against all four dengue virus serotypes, given as two doses three months apart to people aged 4 to 60, with no need for prior-infection screening.
  • The vaccine was approved by India's drug regulator in July 2026 after trials involving more than 28,000 participants, including a Phase III study in the Indian population; it is already approved in over 40 countries.
  • India carries nearly one-third of the global dengue burden, with reported cases up more than 11-fold in two decades — but experts caution vaccination must complement mosquito control, not replace it.

A Distribution Deal for India's First Dengue Shot

India's first dengue vaccine is a step closer to reaching patients. Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India has formalised an exclusive distribution agreement with Dr Reddy's Laboratories, under which the Hyderabad-based drugmaker will promote and distribute Qdenga in the private market for paediatric and adult vaccination in India, The Hindu BusinessLine reported.

Qdenga is expected to be available in the first half of 2027, initially through private healthcare settings, according to infectious disease experts tracking the rollout. Takeda already has a manufacturing tie-up with Indian vaccine maker Biological E, signed in 2024, to expand production of the shot.

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation granted marketing authorisation for Qdenga in July 2026, making it the first dengue vaccine approved in India for the prevention of dengue disease in individuals aged 4 to 60.

How Qdenga Works

Qdenga (TAK-003) is a live, attenuated tetravalent vaccine developed using recombinant DNA technology, built on a dengue virus type-2 backbone with structural proteins from the other three serotypes — giving it coverage against all four dengue virus types, DENV-1 through DENV-4. It is administered as two 0.5 ml subcutaneous injections, three months apart.

Crucially, it can be given regardless of whether a person has previously had dengue — no pre-vaccination blood test is required. That distinguishes it from Sanofi's Dengvaxia, which is not approved in India and is recommended only for people with prior dengue infection, due to concerns about increased risk of severe dengue in some recipients without previous exposure.

The Indian approval rested on Takeda's global clinical development programme: 19 Phase I, II and III trials involving more than 28,000 participants across dengue-endemic and non-endemic regions, plus the Phase III DEN-302 trial conducted in India assessing safety and immune response in people aged 4 to 60. Long-term data collected over seven years showed continued protection against infection and hospitalisation across all four serotypes, the company said. Qdenga has also received WHO prequalification, making it eligible for procurement by agencies such as UNICEF.

The Scale of the Problem

The need is difficult to overstate. The World Health Organisation reported a record 14.4 million dengue cases and 11,201 deaths worldwide in 2024, including 232,425 cases and 233 deaths in India. Takeda says India accounts for nearly one-third of the global dengue burden, with all four virus serotypes circulating simultaneously in several parts of the country. Reported Indian cases have risen more than 11-fold over two decades, driven by rapid urbanisation, climate change and expanding mosquito habitats.

A recent Parliamentary Committee on Health recommended considering the dengue vaccine for India's Universal Immunization Program. "This reflects the growing recognition of dengue as a significant public health challenge," said Mahender Nayak, Takeda's Head of Intercontinental Markets. The company said that while inclusion in the public immunisation programme remains a long-term ambition, private-market availability through Dr Reddy's will give eligible individuals a pathway to access the vaccine once it launches.

"Qdenga can help reduce disease severity and hospitalizations, but it is unlikely to prevent outbreaks as long as the mosquito vector continues to circulate."

— Divya K.S., infectious diseases specialist, Apollo Hospitals

What to Watch

Experts stress that the vaccine is one tool, not a silver bullet: vector control, surveillance and community awareness remain essential, since no vaccine can eradicate dengue while mosquitoes circulate. Pricing in the private market — still undisclosed — will determine how many Indians can actually access the shot in 2027. Meanwhile, Hyderabad-based Indian Immunologicals is developing its own dengue vaccine candidate and preparing mid-stage clinical trials, which could eventually bring a homegrown alternative.

For the millions of Indians — and NRIs visiting family during monsoon season — who live with dengue as an annual threat, the arrival of a first vaccine is a genuine milestone. Whether it reaches beyond private hospitals into the public programme will decide how much of a milestone it becomes.
